definition: Idolatrous means worshipping someone or something excessively, as if it were a god — a word with a built-in warning.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word idolatrous. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know idolatrous should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The franchise's most idolatrous fans refused to admit the new film had a single flaw.
Admiring is healthy appreciation that still sees flaws; idolatrous devotion has crossed the line into treating a person like a god.
Cultish goes even further than idolatrous, suggesting an entire closed group organized around blind worship.

Worshipful means showing reverent, awed adoration, as if before something divine -- but the word itself passes no judgment: a worshipful hush in a cathedral can be perfectly fitting. Idolatrous is worshipful devotion plus a verdict -- the word itself declares that the admiration has gone inappropriately far and turned a person into a god.

Fanatical means devoted beyond all reason, and it measures pure intensity -- a fanatical jogger or fan is simply extreme about the thing. Idolatrous says something more specific: the devotion has become worship, treating a person or thing as a god. Fanatical describes how hard the devotion runs; idolatrous accuses it of the wrong shape.

When chef Duval opened his third restaurant, his line cooks stopped tasting the food before it left the kitchen.
"If he wrote the recipe, it's perfect," one shrugged, and any server who suggested a dish was over-salted got frozen out of the group chat.
A visiting food writer observed that the kitchen's devotion had become idolatrous: the staff no longer served customers — they served a man they had quietly turned into a god.
The cooks' refusal to taste or question anything — treating Duval's word as perfect by definition — is what pushes their devotion past loyalty into idolatrous worship.

Idolatrous is never neutral praise: it signals that admiration has gone inappropriately far, unlike revere and venerable, which describe deep respect that stays healthy and deserved.

Keep it in its own lane among this unit's praise words too — renown is earned fame, adulation is over-the-top gushing, and a commendation is an official act of praise, but idolatrous alone accuses the admirer of treating a person like a god.

Okafor's class spent October on the famous inventor, and at first the unit wrote itself.
The old textbook read like a shrine: every setback was someone else's fault, every rival a villain, every quotation polished to a gleam.
It was Dev who finally said the chapter felt idolatrous, as if the author had set out to build an altar instead of a portrait.
So the class pulled the patent records and letters, and a stranger, more human figure emerged — brilliant, impatient, sometimes wrong.
Admiration survived the archives, Ms.
Okafor pointed out; worship did not.
